title: Which limits are worth paying to relax

blocks.text: A port authority's LP plans berth time, cranes, pilots and dredging. Suppliers and the regulator offer ways to relax some of its rows: extra crane-months, more budget, a waiver that lowers a dredging requirement. Each offer has a cost. Finance wants the offers worth taking, ranked, using the LP's shadow prices instead of a re-solve per offer.
Each offer relaxes one row of the LP, and is a dict with:

items: `"price"`: the row's shadow price $`y`$, in value per row unit (negative for a requirement, a $`\ge`$ row, in a maximization);

`"change"`: $`\Delta`$, how far one unit of the offer moves the row's right-hand side, in row units (a crane-month adds 440 $k of capacity; a waiver that lowers a requirement by 100 has $`\Delta = -100`$);
`"cost"`: what one unit of the offer costs, in the same value units as the objective;
`"units"`: how many units can be bought while the right-hand side stays inside the price's range.

blocks.text: Inside the range the price is exact, so the total net gain of an offer is
Write `worth_buying(offers)` in `relief.py`. Return a list of `(name, gain)` pairs for the offers whose gain is positive, sorted by gain, largest first.

cases.says: an offer's gain is its row's price times the change, less its cost, over all its units, and offers that lose are dropped
one unit bought may move its row by many row units, as a crew-month adds hundreds of $k of capacity
relaxing a requirement lowers its right-hand side, and a negative price times a negative change is a gain
offers are ranked by total gain over their units, not by gain per unit

origin.section: A Negative Price Is the Marginal Cost of a Commitment

concepts: a requirement's negative price is the cost of its last unit, not the average cost of the whole requirement
a price is stated with its unit, its direction and its range, and converted into the partner's units
